slides.title: Welcome to Understanding APIs
slides.narration: Welcome to this Spoken Tutorial on **Understanding APIs**.

slides.title: Learning Objectives
slides.narration:
In this tutorial, you will learn,

• Define what an **API** is and its fundamental purpose.
• Explain the role and importance of **API keys** for authentication and access control.
• Describe the process of how applications send requests to and receive responses from **AI models** via **APIs**.
• Apply the understanding of **API** interaction to interpret basic **AI model** communications.

slides.title: System Requirements
slides.narration: Here I am using a browser on a computer or mobile.

slides.title: Pre-requisite Knowledge
slides.narration: To follow this tutorial, you should have completed Module 1: **Basics of Python**.

slides.title: What is an API? A Digital Handshake
slides.narration:
What is an **API** and why does it matter for building with **AI**?
An **API**, or **Application Programming Interface**, acts as a connector.
It allows different software applications to talk to each other.
Imagine you are at a restaurant.
You tell the waiter your order.
The waiter takes your order to the kitchen.
The kitchen prepares your food.
Then the waiter brings your food back to you.
Here, the waiter is like an **API**.
It takes your request to the **AI model** and brings back the response.
slides.image_prompt: Illustration showing API as a waiter connecting a customer (application) to a kitchen (AI model)

slides.title: API Keys: Your Digital ID
slides.narration:
Now that you know what an **API** is, let's talk about **API keys**.
Think of an **API key** as your digital ID.
It is a unique identifier.
You present this key when you want to use an **AI** service.
This key authenticates you.
It ensures only authorized users can access the **AI models**.
This keeps your interactions secure.
slides.image_prompt: Illustration showing an API key as a digital ID card with a lock icon for security

slides.title: Sending Requests to AI Models
slides.narration:
With your **API key** ready, how do applications talk to **AI models**?
Applications send **requests** to the **AI model**.
These **requests** are like messages.
They ask the **AI model** to perform a specific task.
The **request** is carefully formatted.
This ensures the **AI model** understands what you want.
This is the first step in getting an **AI** to work for you.
slides.image_prompt: Person at laptop, an application sending a message (request) to an AI cloud icon

slides.title: Anatomy of an API Request
slides.narration:
Let's look at what makes up an **API request**.
Every **request** has an **endpoint**.
This is the specific address of the **AI** service you want to use.
Then there are **headers**.
**Headers** contain important metadata.
This includes your **API key** for authentication.
Finally, there is the **payload**.
The **payload** is the actual input data you send to the **AI model**.
For example, it could be your **prompt** for generating text.
slides.image_prompt: Illustration showing the components of an API request: endpoint, headers, and payload as distinct blocks

slides.title: Receiving AI-Generated Responses
slides.narration:
After sending a **request**, you wait for a **response**.
The **AI model** processes your input.
Then it sends back its output as a **response**.
This **response** is also structured data.
Applications receive this data.
They then parse and interpret it.
This is how you get the **AI's** generated text or image.
Understanding the **response** format is crucial.
slides.image_prompt: Person at laptop, receiving structured data (response) from an AI cloud icon

slides.title: Demo: A Vague AI Request
slides.narration:
Now let's see a demo of an **API request**.
Here is a simple, but vague, request to an **AI model**.
Notice how the input is not very specific.
See what kind of **response** we get.
The **response** might be general or unhelpful.
Think about why this input is not ideal.
This shows the importance of clear communication with **AI**.
slides.image_prompt: Screen close-up: user typing 'Here is a simple, but vague, request...'

slides.title: Demo: An Improved AI Request
slides.narration:
With that in mind, let's look at an improved **API request**.
Here, the **prompt** is much more detailed.
We are giving the **AI model** clear instructions.
Observe the difference in the **response**.
The **AI** provides a more relevant and useful output.
This demonstrates the power of well-structured input.
Good input leads to better **AI** results.
slides.image_prompt: Screen close-up: user typing 'Here, the prompt is much more detailed...'

slides.title: Comparing Vague vs. Improved
slides.narration:
Let's compare the vague and improved **requests** side-by-side.
See the clear difference in the input.
The improved **request** specifies the format.
It also adds more context.
This directly impacts the quality of the **AI's response**.
Structured input guides the **AI model** better.
This skill is vital for effective **AI** interaction.
slides.image_prompt: Side-by-side: vague prompt output vs improved prompt output

slides.title: Summary: Key Takeaways
slides.narration:
Let us summarize what we learned.
We defined what an **API** is and its purpose.
We understood the role of **API keys** for security.
Then we covered how applications send **requests**.
Finally, we saw how to receive and interpret **AI responses**.

slides.title: Assignment: Practice Your Skills
slides.narration:
Now as an assignment,
Try sending a simple **API request** to a public **AI** service.
For example, use a text generation **API**.
Experiment with both vague and specific **prompts**.
Compare the results.
